The invisibility cloak was fabricated on a photonic chip made of borosilicate material using femtosecond laser direct writing.
The cloak was able to conceal a structure of size 0.44 mm × 0.35 mm inside the chip.
Up to 5,000 waveguides were fabricated in three dimensions to create the cloak structure.
The optimal pitch (spacing) between the waveguides for the best cloaking performance was found to be 21 μm.
The cloak demonstrated a three-dimensional cloaking capability, with a tolerance for viewing angles spanning 8.0° laterally and 6.7° vertically.
The normalized cross correlation between the input and output images reached a peak of 0.986 at the optimal 21 μm pitch, indicating high-quality image transfer through the cloak.
Tomography analysis was used to visualize the evolution of the light field in the cloak, showing that most of the light circumvents the cloaked area along the waveguides.

The authors suggest that the printed invisibility cloak on a photonic chip could enable novel applications in classical and quantum integrated photonics, as well as in deep space exploration and biological sensing.

Imperfect collective bending of the waveguides may introduce site-dependent length differences and differential phases, which can be addressed by setting the length difference to be an integral multiple of 2π during fabrication.
The size of the hidden structure that can be effectively cloaked is limited by the bending loss introduced with decreasing curvature radius of the waveguides.
The researchers used a curvature radius of 85.9 mm to cloak a structure of size 0.44 mm × 0.35 mm on the photonic chip.
The cloak was able to conceal the inner structure so well that it remained invisible even at large viewing angles that affected the image transmission.
The output power distribution in the light cone showed a radiational decreasing tendency from the center to the edge, which visually agreed with the decreasing clarity of the output image.

The authors mention that the printed cloak allows backdoor operations like swap or coupling, which could be isolated from observers, representing an emerging problem of information security and hacking on a photonic chip.
The researchers used a commercial Beam Propagation Method software to simulate the light field evolution in the cloak structure prior to the experimental demonstration.
